paragraphs: Group decisions require people to coordinate, even when they cannot directly communicate. In that situation, someone’s actions become evidence about what they intend to do. The paper develops a Bayesian account of this process around conformity: the commonly observed tendency for group members to align their behavior. Its goal is to explain collective decision making through probabilistic reasoning about others.

The framework accommodates different levels of theory of mind. At a simpler level, a person infers another person’s hidden intention. More elaborate reasoning considers how capable others are of choosing good actions and how their choices might depend on one’s own behavior. The authors show that their conformity-based framework can express any level of this reasoning.

They demonstrate the framework’s viability in two human experiments: a consensus task involving 120 participants and a volunteer’s dilemma involving 29, each under multiple conditions. These demonstrations support its usefulness for studying distinct coordination problems. The contribution connects conformity with increasingly elaborate reasoning about other people within a single Bayesian framework.
neurips-2019-a-bayesian-theory-of-confor.tldr: A Bayesian framework uses conformity to model different levels of reasoning about others in collective decisions.

paragraphs: Distributionally robust learning accounts for uncertainty about the distribution behind training data. Wasserstein-based formulations can often be rewritten as exact convex optimization problems, making standard solvers applicable. However, the paper identifies a practical obstacle: general-purpose interior-point solvers can make these formulations difficult to use on large learning problems. Having a convex formulation does not by itself make computation affordable.

The authors develop a first-order framework for a class of distributionally robust logistic regression problems. Their method is a linearized proximal version of ADMM, designed around an objective containing one smooth component and two nonsmooth components that cannot be separated. This structure motivates a specialized iterative algorithm instead of relying entirely on a general-purpose solver.

The paper proves a sublinear convergence rate and evaluates the method in three experiments using synthetic and real data. It reports reaching the same accuracy up to more than 800 times faster than the standard solver. That reported speedup concerns the evaluated problems; the broader contribution is a convergence-supported approach to making this robust regression formulation computationally practical.
neurips-2019-a-first-order-algorithmic-f.tldr: A specialized first-order algorithm solves Wasserstein-robust logistic regression with proven convergence and substantial reported speedups.

paragraphs: Bayesian Layers makes uncertainty modeling available through replacements for familiar neural network layers. The module treats deterministic and stochastic functions within one interface, so researchers can compose them into larger architectures. Its design aims to speed up experimentation while using the underlying neural network system to support computation at scale.

The abstraction covers several places where uncertainty can enter a model: weights in Bayesian neural networks, pre-activation units through dropout, activations through stochastic output layers, and entire functions through Gaussian processes. Reversible layers can also propagate uncertainty from inputs to outputs. Code examples illustrate architectures including Bayesian recurrent networks, deep Gaussian processes, and flow-based models.

The demonstrations include fitting a five-billion-parameter Bayesian Transformer on 512 TPUv2 cores for machine translation uncertainty, plus a Bayesian dynamics model for planning. The authors also show integration with Edward2 for probabilistic programming involving stochastic processes. Together, these examples illustrate the module’s range and scalability, with the central contribution being a shared software abstraction for building uncertainty-aware models.
neurips-2019-bayesian-layers-a-module-fo.tldr: Bayesian Layers provides composable neural network components for experimenting with uncertainty across multiple model families.

paragraphs: Attention helps a model build representations by assigning different importance to its inputs. This paper proposes Compositional De-Attention, or CoDA, which expands the operations available when combining input vectors. The model learns whether a vector should be added, subtracted, or nullified. That gives it a way to express different kinds of contribution while constructing a representation.

The approach uses both similarity and dissimilarity when calculating affinity scores. Negative affinity is therefore part of the representation-building mechanism. Subtraction can express a contribution with the opposite direction, while nullification can remove a vector’s contribution. The authors motivate these choices as a way to make the mechanism more expressive than ordinary token reweighting.

CoDA is evaluated on six language task families: question answering, retrieval and ranking, natural language inference, translation, sentiment analysis, and text-to-code generation. The authors report promising results, including state-of-the-art performance on several tasks or datasets. These findings support the usefulness of richer compositional operations across varied language applications, without establishing that every evaluated task benefits equally.
neurips-2019-compositional-de-attention-.tldr: CoDA extends attention with learned addition, subtraction, and nullification, achieving strong results across several language tasks.

paragraphs: Adaptive Bayesian quadrature estimates integrals by choosing where to evaluate a function based on values already observed. This choice is controlled by an acquisition function that changes as information accumulates. The abstract describes favorable empirical comparisons with Monte Carlo integration on medium-dimensional problems, where non-adaptive quadrature struggles. Yet this dependence on earlier observations also makes the method difficult to analyze mathematically.

The paper introduces a concept called weak adaptivity to establish guarantees for a broad class of these methods. Using this concept, the authors prove consistency: the covered methods converge toward the correct integral as the procedure progresses. They also derive convergence rates, providing information about the speed of that approach to the target.

The rates are explicitly described as informative but not tight, so they need not capture the best possible behavior. The main significance is that a large, flexible family of adaptive rules gains theoretical support. Practitioners can develop empirically efficient methods within that family while retaining a consistency guarantee, connecting adaptive numerical performance with mathematical reliability.
neurips-2019-convergence-guarantees-for-.tldr: Weak adaptivity enables consistency proofs and informative convergence rates for a broad class of adaptive Bayesian integration methods.

paragraphs: The vine copula autoencoder turns an autoencoder into a generative model through a three-step construction. First, an encoder compresses high-dimensional observations into a smaller representation. Next, vine copulas estimate the joint distribution of these encoded observations. Finally, that estimated distribution is combined with the decoder to produce a model capable of generating data.

The key division of work is between learning a useful representation and modeling how encoded observations are distributed. The autoencoder supplies the compression and reconstruction machinery, while the copula component supplies the distribution in the compressed space. The authors state that this procedure can convert any already trained autoencoder into a flexible generative model at low computational cost.

This offers an alternative to generative approaches whose training can be difficult or whose latent-space assumptions can be restrictive. Experiments on MNIST, Street View House Numbers, and CelebFaces Attributes show results competitive with standard baselines. The reported finding supports the practicality of this modular construction; it does not claim consistent superiority over every competing generative approach.
neurips-2019-copulas-as-high-dimensional.tldr: Vine copula autoencoders model encoded-data distributions to turn trained autoencoders into flexible, competitive generative models.

paragraphs: Instrumental variable analysis helps estimate causal effects when randomization or complete control of confounding factors is unavailable. Existing methods become difficult to apply when effects are complex or when treatments and instruments have many dimensions. DeepGMM addresses these challenges by reformulating the generalized method of moments, an approach that estimates relationships through statistical conditions the model should satisfy.

The central contribution is a variational reformulation using optimal inverse-covariance weighting. It allows the algorithm to manage very many moment conditions efficiently. The authors also develop practical optimization and model-selection techniques, connecting the mathematical formulation to a computationally tractable procedure that can handle large datasets.

In numerical evaluations, DeepGMM matches the best tuned methods in standard settings and continues to work in high-dimensional settings where even recent alternatives fail. These results indicate that its benefits become particularly relevant as the estimation problem grows more complex. The paper’s stated contribution combines a new formulation with practical training choices, rather than relying on the reformulation alone.
neurips-2019-deep-generalized-method-of-.tldr: DeepGMM reformulates instrumental-variable estimation to handle many statistical constraints and challenging high-dimensional causal problems.

paragraphs: Distributionally robust optimization trains against uncertainty about the data distribution. A central design choice is how to measure which alternative distributions belong to the uncertainty set. This paper studies sets defined through maximum mean discrepancy, or MMD, adding another approach alongside formulations based on phi-divergences and Wasserstein distances.

The authors show that MMD-based robust optimization is roughly equivalent to regularization using a Hilbert-space norm. This links protection against distributional uncertainty with a familiar way of controlling model complexity. The connection also yields another proof of a generalization bound for Gaussian kernel ridge regression, and the reasoning behind that proof suggests a new regularizer.

The analysis extends beyond kernel methods through a broadly applicable approximation of MMD-based robust optimization. The authors show that this approximation generalizes recent variance-based regularization work. The contribution is therefore both an interpretation and a methodological extension: it connects robustness, regularization, and generalization through one distributional framework while preserving the qualified nature of the equivalence.
neurips-2019-distributionally-robust-opt.tldr: MMD-based robust optimization connects distributional uncertainty with norm regularization, kernel generalization bounds, and variance-based penalties.

paragraphs: Online learning with expert advice becomes more complicated when some experts are unavailable. The general sleeping-experts problem allows experts to disappear and later return, and existing results suggest that achieving optimal regret against a fully adversarial environment is computationally difficult. This paper studies a restricted availability pattern: once an expert becomes unavailable, it never returns.

The authors call this setting dying experts and analyze two versions. In one, the learner knows the order in which experts will disappear; in the other, that order is unknown. Both versions use ranking regret as their performance benchmark. Separating these cases makes advance knowledge of availability an explicit part of the learning problem.

For each case, the paper provides matching upper and lower bounds in the fully adversarial setting. The lower bounds establish unavoidable difficulty, while the upper bounds show what a learner can achieve. New computationally efficient algorithms attain those upper bounds. Thus, permanent disappearance defines a setting where optimal ranking-regret guarantees and efficient computation can be obtained together.
neurips-2019-dying-experts-efficient-alg.tldr: When unavailable experts never return, efficient algorithms achieve optimal ranking regret whether or not their disappearance order is known.

paragraphs: In multi-agent reinforcement learning, agents can exchange information to improve their decisions, but communication creates overhead. This paper introduces Variance Based Control, or VBC, as a simple technique for making those exchanges more efficient. The approach focuses on the content of exchanged messages during training and on reducing the noisy component of that communication.

VBC limits the variance of messages passed between agents. The authors describe this constraint as a way to suppress noise while preserving useful information that agents can use to perform better. The important connection is between message variability and communication quality: controlling the former is intended to make the latter more effective without discarding its useful contribution.

Across multiple multi-agent reinforcement learning benchmarks, the method reports communication overhead two to ten times lower than state-of-the-art algorithms, together with better overall performance. These are empirical findings from the evaluated benchmarks. They indicate that reducing noisy communication can improve both communication efficiency and task outcomes, rather than requiring a tradeoff between those two goals in these experiments.
neurips-2019-efficient-communication-in-.tldr: Controlling message variance during training reduces communication overhead and improves performance on multiple multi-agent reinforcement learning benchmarks.

paragraphs: This paper studies how gradient descent trains deep linear residual networks, focusing on the interaction between depth and initialization. The authors introduce zero-asymmetric initialization, abbreviated ZAS. Its motivation is to avoid stable manifolds of saddle points: configurations associated with saddle points that can obstruct progress toward a good solution.

For an arbitrary target matrix, the authors prove that gradient descent under ZAS reaches an epsilon-optimal point in O(L³ log(1/epsilon)) iterations, where L is network depth. The bound grows polynomially with depth and logarithmically with the inverse of the requested accuracy. It therefore gives an explicit relationship between network size, optimization precision, and the number of iterations.

The paper contrasts this guarantee with an existing exponential-in-depth convergence-time result for standard Xavier or near-identity initialization. Together, these results demonstrate why residual structure and initialization matter for optimizing deep linear networks, especially at large depths. The guarantee concerns this particular linear residual setting and the proposed initialization, which are central to the result’s meaning.
neurips-2019-global-convergence-of-gradi.tldr: Zero-asymmetric initialization gives gradient descent a polynomial-in-depth convergence guarantee for deep linear residual networks.

paragraphs: Implicit Semantic Data Augmentation, or ISDA, augments training through deep feature representations. The motivating observation is that some directions in feature space correspond to meaningful changes, such as adding sunglasses or changing backgrounds. Moving representations along these directions can supply useful variation that complements conventional image transformations such as flipping, translation, and rotation.

The method estimates a feature covariance matrix for each class during training. This captures variation within the class and defines a zero-mean Gaussian distribution for feature perturbations. Instead of explicitly constructing all those augmented samples, ISDA minimizes an upper bound on their expected cross-entropy loss. The resulting objective can be expressed as a robust cross-entropy loss.

This implicit calculation adds negligible computational cost to ordinary training according to the authors. Experiments report consistent generalization improvements for ResNets and DenseNets across datasets including CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet. The central contribution is an efficient way to account for semantic feature variation directly in the training objective, making augmentation possible without separately materializing the perturbed examples.
neurips-2019-implicit-semantic-data-augm.tldr: ISDA incorporates semantic feature perturbations into a robust training loss, improving generalization with negligible reported overhead.

paragraphs: Kernel instrumental variable regression addresses causal estimation when input and output measurements are confounded. The abstract describes identification using an instrument that directly influences the input and is conditionally independent of the output given the input and unmeasured confounder. This instrumental-variable structure supplies a route to estimating causal relationships from observational data.

Classic two-stage least squares simplifies the problem by using linear relationships. The proposed KIV method generalizes that approach to nonlinear functions represented in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces. It retains the instrumental-variable estimation strategy while allowing richer relationships among the instrument, input, and output.

The authors prove consistency under mild assumptions and derive conditions for matching the minimax-optimal convergence rate of unconfounded, single-stage kernel regression. Their analysis also yields an efficient allocation of training samples between the two stages. Experiments report better performance than state-of-the-art alternatives for nonparametric instrumental-variable regression. The rate comparison is conditional on the derived requirements, while the experimental results support the practical value of the nonlinear formulation.
neurips-2019-kernel-instrumental-variabl.tldr: KIV extends two-stage instrumental-variable regression to nonlinear kernel models, with consistency and conditional optimal-rate guarantees.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to recover the directed structure of a Bayesian network from data accessed through a black-box model. The algorithm obtains information by asking conditional-probability queries. Its central assumption is a form of simplicity in the conditional probability tables associated with network nodes, which the authors call low rankness.

The authors connect this representation property to the Fourier transformation of real-valued set functions. That connection supports a method for learning the exact directed structure of a low-rank Bayesian network using few queries. The contribution links a constraint on how local probabilities are represented to the larger problem of recovering the network’s directed relationships.

The paper formally proves correct recovery, polynomial running time, and polynomial sample requirements as a function of the number of nodes. It also describes further efficiency improvements when observational data are available. These guarantees apply to the stated low-rank setting and query-based access model, making the representation assumption an essential part of why efficient exact recovery is possible.
neurips-2019-learning-bayesian-networks-.tldr: A query-based method exactly recovers low-rank Bayesian network structure with polynomial time and sample requirements.

paragraphs: Model-based reinforcement learning often trains an explicit predictor of the environment and then uses it to help an agent act. This paper asks whether a useful world model can emerge through another training pressure. Its motivation is that predictive abilities can arise as a side effect of optimization whose objective does not explicitly reward accurate forecasts.

The proposed modification is observational dropout. During reinforcement learning, the agent’s access to observations of the real environment is restricted at individual time steps. These gaps create pressure to develop an internal world model that supplies missing information. The agent therefore learns under a task objective while facing reduced access to direct environmental evidence.

The authors show that the resulting world model can help the agent acquire key skills needed to perform well, despite not being explicitly trained to predict the future. The finding establishes a possible route to useful internal modeling through observation constraints. Its significance is that the training circumstances themselves can encourage predictive representations without a dedicated forward-prediction loss.
neurips-2019-learning-to-predict-without.tldr: Restricting an agent’s observations can encourage a useful world model to emerge without an explicit future-prediction objective.

paragraphs: This paper augments recurrent neural networks with an external memory represented by another deep neural network. The memory is conceived as a function that can adapt quickly. Its stored information is expressed through the function’s parameters, making changes to that function the central operation for recording new information.

Reading and writing have concrete meanings in this design. To read, the model passes a key vector through the memory network and receives a value vector. To write, it updates the memory network’s parameters so that the desired information is encoded. The authors use training and algorithmic techniques from metalearning to make this neural memory update possible in one shot.

The resulting memory-augmented model achieves strong performance across learning problems ranging from supervised question answering to reinforcement learning. These results support the usefulness of rapidly adaptable functions as external memory mechanisms. The conceptual contribution is to connect memory access with neural function evaluation and memory storage with learned parameter adaptation, bringing metalearning directly into how a recurrent model retains information.
neurips-2019-metalearned-neural-memory-2.tldr: A metalearned neural network serves as external memory, reading through function evaluation and writing through rapid parameter updates.

paragraphs: Online continual learning asks a model to learn from an ongoing data stream with a single pass through incoming data. Replay helps preserve earlier knowledge by revisiting stored examples or generating substitutes. This paper focuses on which examples should be replayed, challenging the usual practice of selecting them randomly.

Maximal Interfered Retrieval chooses examples whose predictions are expected to suffer most from the impending parameter update. The selection criterion therefore uses anticipated damage to earlier knowledge to guide rehearsal. This makes replay responsive to what the next learning step threatens, rather than treating all available memories as equally useful at that moment.

The authors formulate this criterion for both experience replay from stored examples and generative replay. They report consistent performance gains and greatly reduced forgetting. The contribution is a controlled sampling strategy that can be applied to both forms of memory, showing that replay effectiveness depends on the choice of examples as well as on having a replay mechanism at all.
neurips-2019-online-continual-learning-w.tldr: Replaying examples most threatened by an upcoming update improves continual-learning performance and reduces forgetting.

paragraphs: The Poisson-randomized gamma dynamical system models count tensors observed over time. Its design favors sparse and bursty patterns, making those characteristics part of its inductive bias. The model represents evolving hidden structure through an alternating sequence of discrete Poisson states and continuous gamma states.

This alternating construction is designed to make inference mathematically convenient and computationally tractable. It yields closed-form conditional distributions for every variable using the Bessel distribution and a newly introduced shifted confluent hypergeometric distribution. The contribution therefore includes both a model for temporal count data and a probabilistic construction that makes working with its hidden variables manageable.

The authors compare related models on real-world text, international-event, and neural-spike data. A sparse version allows continuous gamma states to equal exactly zero. It often achieves better predictive performance than other models and is reported to be uniquely capable, within these comparisons, of recovering hidden structures concentrated in narrow periods of time. Exact-zero states are thus tied to the model’s ability to represent sharply localized activity.
neurips-2019-poisson-randomized-gamma-dy.tldr: Alternating Poisson and gamma hidden states provide tractable modeling of sparse, bursty count data and temporally localized structure.

paragraphs: The paper introduces q-means, a quantum clustering algorithm based on a robust version of k-means. It aims to accelerate clustering while retaining convergence and precision guarantees similar to that robust classical procedure. The authors also design a method for selecting initial cluster centroids equivalent to classical k-means++ initialization.

The stated speedup is exponential in the number of data points compared with classical k-means. This identifies the particular aspect of dataset size in which the runtime improves. The paper provides a detailed runtime analysis and separately describes the running time for well-clusterable datasets, connecting the computational analysis to the structure of the clustering problem.

Numerical simulations on specific datasets accompany the algorithm and theoretical results. Together, these components examine its behavior as well as its computational guarantees. Beyond the clustering method itself, the authors present theorems and tools intended for reuse in other quantum machine learning applications. The central contribution combines quantum acceleration with attention to initialization, convergence, and precision.
neurips-2019-q-means-a-quantum-algorithm.tldr: Q-means offers quantum clustering with an exponential speedup in dataset size and guarantees similar to robust k-means.

paragraphs: A model’s interpretation can be a target of robustness training alongside its predictions. This paper studies that goal through Integrated Gradients, an attribution method that assigns changes in a neural network’s output to changes in its input. The authors develop training objectives intended to make these attributions robust using established robust optimization frameworks.

The objectives generalize earlier objectives designed for robust predictions. For one-layer neural networks, they reduce to classical soft-margin training, connecting the proposed approach to a familiar special case. The paper also extends previous theory and proves close relationships between objectives arising from different robust optimization models.

Experiments demonstrate that the method is effective, while also revealing difficulties that suggest a need for improved optimization methods or neural network architectures. Those observations make the empirical conclusion qualified: robust attribution training shows promise, but the tested formulations also expose unresolved challenges. The contribution brings explanation robustness into a principled training framework and clarifies how it relates to existing approaches to prediction robustness.
neurips-2019-robust-attribution-regulari.tldr: Robust optimization objectives train neural networks for more robust Integrated Gradients attributions while revealing remaining optimization challenges.

paragraphs: RUDDER addresses delayed rewards in finite Markov decision processes. Estimating an action’s value involves both immediate and future rewards, and delayed feedback worsens bias problems in temporal-difference learning and variance problems in Monte Carlo learning. RUDDER aims to redistribute rewards so that expected future rewards become zero, simplifying value estimation to the average immediate reward.

The approach combines reward redistribution with return decomposition through contribution analysis. Redistribution produces decision processes with equivalent returns and the same optimal policies. When the redistribution is optimal, expected future rewards are zero. Contribution analysis recasts the task of decomposing returns as regression, enabling deep learning to help determine how reward should be assigned.

On artificial delayed-reward tasks, the authors report significant speed gains over Monte Carlo learning and exponential gains over Monte Carlo Tree Search, TD(lambda), and reward shaping approaches. Added to a PPO baseline, RUDDER also improves Atari scores, especially in games with delayed rewards. These findings support the practical value of changing reward timing while preserving the underlying optimal-policy objective.
neurips-2019-rudder-return-decomposition.tldr: RUDDER redistributes delayed rewards to simplify value estimation while preserving optimal policies, with strong reported learning-speed gains.

paragraphs: Zero-shot learning recognizes previously unseen classes through semantic descriptions. This paper argues that the visual features used for that recognition deserve attention alongside the mapping between visual and semantic representations. It focuses on finding object regions that distinguish classes, so the model can use informative details as well as the overall object.

The proposed semantic-guided multi-attention model automatically discovers discriminative object parts without human annotations for that localization. It jointly learns global features from the whole object and local features from the detected parts. Semantic descriptions guide categorization, while embedding softmax and class-center triplet losses encourage different classes to spread apart and examples within a class to cluster together.

Experiments on three widely used zero-shot learning benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of the localization component and report a considerable improvement over state-of-the-art results. The findings support combining semantic guidance with learned part discovery. The contribution connects where a model looks with how it organizes class representations, making visual feature learning an explicit part of recognizing unseen categories.
neurips-2019-semantic-guided-multi-atten.tldr: Semantic-guided attention discovers informative object parts and combines local and global features to improve zero-shot recognition.

paragraphs: Sequence generators commonly commit to an order such as producing tokens from left to right. This paper treats that order as something the model can learn. It proposes a generator that constructs an output by inserting tokens in arbitrary order, expanding the ways a sequence can be assembled during decoding.

The distinction is between the arrangement of the finished sequence and the order of decisions used to build it. An insertion-based model can create the final output through different sequences of token insertions. Its training procedure determines the decoding order, so generation is no longer tied to a single predefined progression through output positions.

Experiments show the model outperforming fixed-order models on multiple sequence-generation tasks, including machine translation, image-to-LaTeX conversion, and image captioning. These tasks provide evidence that learning generation order can be useful across different sources and kinds of output. The stated result concerns the evaluated comparisons; the broader methodological contribution is making construction order part of what a sequence model learns.
neurips-2019-sequence-modeling-with-unco.tldr: A token-insertion model learns its generation order and outperforms fixed-order models on several sequence-generation tasks.

paragraphs: This paper develops a theoretical framework for bounding learning risk in the presence of adversaries. The authors first introduce a transport map between distributions, allowing the adversarial learning problem to be expressed as a minimax statistical learning problem. This reframing provides a common mathematical structure for analyzing how a learner performs against adverse changes.

Within that structure, they prove a risk bound expressed through covering numbers, which measure the complexity of the relevant function class. The proof uses a weak form of a Lipschitz condition. The framework applies to multiclass classification and includes commonly used losses such as hinge loss and ramp loss.

The authors illustrate the method by deriving adversarial risk bounds for support vector machines and deep neural networks. These bounds contain two data-dependent terms that can be optimized to pursue adversarial robustness. The contribution therefore goes beyond a change in mathematical viewpoint: it produces bounds whose components suggest quantities to control during learning, under the stated theoretical conditions.
neurips-2019-theoretical-analysis-of-adv.tldr: A minimax reformulation yields adversarial risk bounds with data-dependent terms that can guide robustness optimization.

paragraphs: BERT’s usefulness across language tasks raises a question about what its internal representations contain. This paper investigates that question through both qualitative and quantitative analysis. Its focus is the geometry of linguistic information: how meaning and grammatical structure appear in the model’s internal representations.

The authors find that semantic and syntactic features seem to occupy separate subspaces. They also identify evidence of a fine-grained geometric representation of word senses, suggesting that distinctions in meaning have structure within the representation space. These observations are presented as evidence about BERT’s organization, preserving the exploratory character of the findings.

The study examines syntax in both attention matrices and individual word embeddings, giving empirical descriptions at two different locations within the model. A mathematical argument accompanies those descriptions to help explain their geometry. Together, the analyses connect visible patterns with quantitative measurements and theoretical reasoning. The contribution is a more concrete account of how a successful language model may internally organize meaning and syntax.
neurips-2019-visualizing-and-measuring-t.tldr: Geometric analyses of BERT find evidence of structured word senses and apparently separate semantic and syntactic subspaces.
